newsitem.title: BULGARIA: REFORMERS FORECAST SPLIT IN BULGARIAN RULING PARTY.
newsitem.headline: REFORMERS FORECAST SPLIT IN BULGARIAN RULING PARTY.

text.p: Reformers in Bulgaria's ruling Socialists said on Thursday a party split was inevitable after their humiliation in the first round of presidential elections.
Andrei Raichev, a leading member of the party's reformist Union for Social Democracy wing (USD), said the Socialists' divided leadership would finally split after Sunday's second round of voting.
"The process of splitting the Socialist Party will start after the election," Raichev told Reuters after a USD news conference. "It is impossible for its different parts to cohabit any longer."
Turnout for last Sunday's first round was the lowest in Bulgaria's post-communist history, and protest candidates were the only ones who saw their share of support grow.
Opposition candidate Petar Stoyanov polled 43.93 percent, 17 points ahead of the Socialist Ivan Marazov, who took 26.92 percent.
"Prime Minister Zhan Videnov should be ousted from both his posts, as Socialist Party chairman and as head of the government," Raichev said.
Rossen Karadimov of the USD leadership criticised the government for delaying structural reforms and said uncertainty about the future had turned Socialist voters away.

"The country's economic reform should have started a year and a half earlier as than the social price would have been much lower and the transition would have been less painful for the people," Karadimov told reporters.
Videnov on Tuesday ruled out changes in the cabinet or the party leadership, saying a reshuffle now would only worsen the crisis.
The Socialists have a secure majority in parliament, while the more ceremonial post of president is already held by the opposition Union of Democratic Forces.

As voters prepare to choose between the leftist populism offered by Marazov and the pro-market liberal Stoyanov, an International Monetary Fund mission is discussing terms for release of a twice-postponed $115 million credit to help stave off debt default.
Gross domestic product (GDP) is now expected to fall by between 8.1 percent and 10.5 percent this year and by 2.0 to 4.0 percent in 1997.
This compares with a government budget revision made in July which forecast zero GDP growth this year, down from an originally planned three percent growth.
The IMF postponed the $115 million second tranche of its standby credit last month until the government fulfilled its pledges to close down loss-making state enterprises and speed up privatisation.
The central bank has placed 14 banks in receivership in a bid to stabilise the crumbling financial system and has sought bankruptcy for five of them through the courts.

The government, struggling to avoid default on $10 billion of foreign debt payments, has offered for privatisation some 20 major state industrial enterprises hoping to raise around $1 billion in the next few months.

Many traditional Socialist voters more concerned with falling living standards and rising prices stayed home on Sunday or voted for maverick populist George Ganchev, who polled a startling 21.8 percent. Talks between him and the Socialists have so far failed to produce a second round deal.
Turnout of 63 percent was well below the 75 percent who voted in parliamentary elections won by the Socialists in December 1994.
